passages.title: Growing faith amid suffering leads into hope for relief and prayer for good work
passages.summary: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write again to the Thessalonians. They thank God that the readers’ faith grows and their love increases. They boast of the readers’ endurance in persecutions. They say God will repay the afflicters and give relief to the afflicted. That will happen when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his angels. Those who do not obey the good news will be punished. He will be glorified in his saints on that day. The writers pray that God will count the readers worthy of their calling.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Thessalonica as one city point. The map has no point for the temple of God.

lds.text: Why does promised relief lead into prayer for continued good work?

contextNote.title: Growing faith amid suffering leads into hope for relief and prayer for good work
contextNote.text: Verses 6–10 promise relief at the Lord’s revealing, which is still future. Verse 11 says what the writers ask for the time between. “To this end” ties the prayer to that day. They ask God to count the readers worthy of their calling. They ask him to complete every good desire and work of faith with power. The work is the readers’, and the power is God’s. Verse 12 gives the aim: the name of Jesus glorified in them.

passages.title: Claims that the day has arrived must answer the instruction already received
passages.summary: Paul asks them not to be shaken by a letter said to be his. Such a message says the day of the Lord has already come. That day will not come before the rebellion and the man of sin. That man will sit in God’s temple and claim to be God. Something now restrains him. The Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth. Those who refused to love the truth will be deceived. Paul thanks God for choosing the readers and tells them to stand firm.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Thessalonica as one city point. The map has no point for the temple of God.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson applies falling away to the Great Apostasy before Christ's return. Why can a message claimed to come from the teachers still require testing?

contextNote.title: Claims that the day has arrived must answer the instruction already received
contextNote.text: Verse 2 names three ways a false report could come: spirit, word, or letter. Any of them might claim the writers’ authority. Verse 5 reminds them that Paul told them these things in person. Verse 15 gives the test that follows. They are to hold what the writers taught, by word or by letter. A new claim is measured against that teaching. Verse 3:17 adds a safeguard: Paul’s own handwriting marks every letter.

passages.title: Refusal of work calls for correction that still recognizes a brother
passages.summary: Paul asks for prayer that the Lord’s word will spread quickly. The Lord is faithful and will guard them. He commands them to withdraw from any brother who refuses to work. He worked night and day and ate no one’s bread for free. He gave the rule that one who will not work should not eat. Some are busybodies and should work quietly. Anyone who ignores this letter should be noted and avoided. Paul signs with his own hand.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Thessalonica as one city point. The map has no point for the temple of God.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches useful work for oneself and people in need. How does treating the person as a brother limit the aim of separation?

contextNote.title: Refusal of work calls for correction that still recognizes a brother
contextNote.text: Verse 14 tells them to note a disobedient person and keep away. The stated aim is that he be ashamed. Verse 15 limits how far that goes. He is not to be counted an enemy. He is to be admonished, and the word used for him is still “brother.” Verse 6 used the same word at the start of the instruction. The distance is meant to correct him, not to disown him.
